# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Omar, Faith and Trevor all weigh the price against what logs cost them now, Lena and Bill both object to a per-site fee stacking up across jobs, the two group names are plain, and my free-trial ask and Sandra's legal-record worry don't fit either group, so leaving them alone is right.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all seven speak to the price.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) sits apart from the commitment step (20-21), where my first real step was already 'start a paid pilot on one site', so it reads like a late afterthought instead of part of how it sells.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20-21 (first real step: a paid pilot on one site) and screen 22 (Offer a pilot?) cover the same ground; screens 3 and 4 also show the identical kicker and question.
founder.missing: Nothing asked what the price is per: I charge per site per month with unlimited users and discounts for multi-site or multi-month terms, and the price screen's wording ('something that cuts the hours on documentation') does not ask for that unit.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It goes from what the daily log costs us now, to what Fresco is worth, to who signs and how long a trial takes, to whether I'd pilot, which is how I'd think it through, though the 'One more thing' screen sits where '3 of 6' should be and the count skips a number.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether it works with Procore or ACC, since our logs have to land there, and how the price scales across all our sites and users rather than one site at a time.

screens.why2: Security review, a Procore check and a trial on one live job are how I talk about selling to a GC, so I read it once and know it's right.
screens.why3: I run these pilots and integration checks with contractors myself, so I know these steps first-hand.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and are my own steps; the belief tests the one that really gates the deal, the live-job trial, and 'or not need it' covers firms that skip it.
screens.why5: The rows are the three steps I gave, unchanged, and the belief about a two-week trial matches how I'd pitch a pilot on one site.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the three purchase steps Keel wrote, it makes sense to pick the one I want tested and put my own estimate on it, and the trial on one live job is the step that really decides our deals.
screens.why2: The three steps are in my words, but 'how long would this step take before it went through' reads oddly for a trial, which runs and ends in a yes or no rather than 'going through', so I read the intro twice.
screens.why3: I run these pilots with GCs myself, so I know about how long a one-site trial takes before the ops lead says yes or no.
screens.why4: The three options are exactly the steps I gave (trial, Procore check, security review), they are distinct, and days/weeks/months covers any honest answer for a trial.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my pick and my 2 weeks, puts the contractor's operations lead as the person who decides, and the 'or not need it' allowance is fair.
screens.instead: Which buying step do you want to test? (A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review) -- How long would that step take from start until they decide to buy? [number] days / weeks / months

screens.why1: Right after who decides, the price and what slows a purchase, the natural last question is what I want the operations lead to actually commit to, and here it closes the commercial section at 6 of 6.
screens.why2: 'First real step' and the hint about time, data, money or a signature are plain, and my answer comes straight out in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask a general contractor for after a demo: a paid pilot on one live site.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right way out for a founder who has no commitment step to test.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'start a paid pilot on one site' word for word and puts it with the operations lead; 'in most cases' and 'now' only frame it as a claim to test.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step I want from the buyer, it makes sense to see that step written back as the belief Keel will test with operations leads.
screens.why2: "Paid pilot on one site" is how I talk about a GC trial, and the line reads cleanly on the first pass.
screens.why3: Whether an ops lead would greenlight a paid pilot on a live job is exactly what I hear on every sales call, so I can judge it from what I know.
screens.why4: The step stays under nine words, and the bar of no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no is clear and matches "in most cases".
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, but the tacked-on "now" drifts a little, because a GC only starts a pilot when a job is running and a site walk is happening, not on the spot.
screens.instead: In most cases the contractor operations lead would start a paid pilot on one site on their next live job.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (a paid pilot on one site), it makes sense to ask whether the study should actually offer it before it goes out.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is plain to me; we pitch every GC on a pilot on one job, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads from this study is my own call about my own sales pipeline.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice, and both chips are clear and distinct.
screens.why5: What I typed was "start a paid pilot on one site", but the line strangers get, "Would you try this for real?", drops both the paid part and the one-site part, so a yes there is a softer signal than the step I named; it also doesn't say whether the line goes to the supers, who don't pay, or only to the ops leads, who do.
screens.instead: Offer the pilot you named? Contractor operations leads who say yes get: "Would you start a paid pilot of this on one of your sites? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who asks my supers the questions belongs right before the link goes out, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The hint packs video, voice, typing, 400 credits and text messages into one paragraph, and it says 'voice' while the interviewer is on video with a face, so I had to read it twice to know what I was locking.
screens.why3: I can play both clips and judge which one a super in his trailer at six o'clock would listen to.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers, each with a five-second sample, and Daphne preselected is a fair default; nothing is missing for this choice.
screens.why5: It still says construction superintendents and the text-message link, and nothing of Fresco leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions on video? (Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s) — hint: people can also read and type; the one you pick is recorded once for 400 credits.

screens.why1: Choosing how the buyers will answer belongs right after picking who asks, just before sending, and Read and tap is the obvious pick for an ops lead answering at a desk between bids.
screens.why2: Video, talking, typing, tapping and 'ready now' are all plain to me, and 'contractors' is how I talk about the GCs I sell to.
screens.why3: I know how my ops leads and CFO-types live: email links, a few minutes at a desk, not a video chat, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI video, text, or let them choose covers the real choices, the three are distinct, and the readiness notes make the trade-off clear; only the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' header looks like a rendering slip.
screens.why5: I typed 'contractor operations lead' as the decider, and the previous screen was about superintendents, so the switch to the generic 'contractors' drifts a little from my words and could leave me unsure which link this is.
screens.instead: How should the contractor operations leads answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne) · Read and tap · Let them choose

screens.why1: Once I've set how the supers and the contractors answer, the next thing is who gets the links, so this is the right moment.
screens.why2: The options read plainly, but I'm running two groups (supers and contractor ops leads) and the screen doesn't say which group this link choice is for, so I'd have to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know which supers and GCs I have by name from our site visits and YC intros, so I can answer this straight off.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel contact list and one open link cover how I'd reach people, and the three don't overlap; 'by name' fits the supers and GCs we've met.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed, and nothing of Fresco or the roles shows to a respondent.
screens.instead: Who gets a link, for the superintendents and for the contractors? (People I know by name / People I found with Keel / One open link I post where they already are)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 'Price: 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month', and the Price card's bar of 6 of 8 shows how far short that is.
screens.why_b2: The tally '2 holding · 1 not holding · 2 did not hold · 1 too few' counts six cards but sits next to '8 people answered', and I have to work out why Price is 'not holding up' while Commitment at 3 of 8 'did not hold' before the counts read cleanly.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, purchase friction and commitment carry my lines word for word, and the other three cards are the price, cost and budget beliefs I set up.
screens.why_b4: The page says who was asked but never what to do: nothing about rethinking the $800-$1,000 price when the hours it replaces hold at a median of 40, or about the trial and pilot both falling short.
screens.why_b5: Every card shows its n and bar, holds at the bar are marked 'at the bar', and ability to pay is honestly 'too few to call' rather than stretched.
screens.instead: Not holding up: only 1 of 8 contractor ops leads value Fresco at $800+ a site a month, though supers spend a median 40 hours a month on the log -- the cost is there but the price isn't landing; test a lower per-site price or sell the hours saved, and shorten the trial since 3 of 8 expect it to take over 2 weeks and only 3 of 8 would start a paid pilot now.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside "5 of 7 spend 30 hours or more per site a month · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar," so I see the verdict and the deciding number together, and I can see it only just clears.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts hours of the daily log per site a month over 7 people, with 5 for and 2 against, and the marker sits at 5 of 7 with the median at 40 hours, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: This is my existing-sacrifice belief, 30 to 60 hours per site a month on the daily log, in my own words.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the cost is real but that willingness to pay is a separate question for the Price card, which is the right next thing to look at given price came back not holding.
screens.why_b5: The small n is flagged ("a lean, not a call"), but "The cost is there" is stated flatly for a result sitting exactly on the bar, and Trevor's 10.9 hours looks converted from a dollar amount without the screen saying so.
screens.instead: Just at the bar, 5 of 7 ops leads put the log at 30+ hours a site a month (median 40), so the time cost likely exceeds $1k; Price said they won't pay that, so sell the hours back, not the software.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside "1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month · bar 6 of 8", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts what each lead would pay per site a month, over 8 people, with my $800 to $1,000 band marked and the bar at 6 of 8; I read it on first look, even though the $800 to under $2,500 bucket is wide.
screens.why_b3: It is my price, $800 to $1,000 per site a month, but the line "would think Fresco worth" is Keel's wording, and this belief was not among the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats that most chose under $500 and sends me to Insights; it doesn't say what to do, though the quotes point at a free first job, per-user rather than per-site pricing, and showing the hours, and it doesn't connect to the sacrifice card where the cost was above my price.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (8 answered, 8 counted), and the screen flags "a small group: a lean, not a call", so it claims nothing beyond what eight leads said.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 8 leads would pay $800 a site, and 5 put it under $500, even though the supers' time it replaces runs above that; the leads asked for a free first job, pricing per super, and proof of the hours saved, so test one of those before you defend $1,000.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number: 1 of 8 named my price or more, and 5 are needed.
screens.why_b2: The four budget sources and the single answer read plainly, but 'your bar · 1 of 1 (at least 2 in 3)' reads at first like the bar was met, when that one answer counts against me.
screens.why_b3: I never typed an ability-to-pay belief; Keel derived it from my $800 to $1,000 price, so I recognise it as mine only through the price.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me to wait but not what to do: find more buyers who would pay $800 or more, or treat this as moot until the price question is fixed.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and 'a lean, not a call' is honest, but the So line says Gordon 'said where the money would come from' without saying his answer, a new budget line, counts against me, and '1 of 1' at the bar softens that.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Gordon named $800 or more, and he would need a new budget line signed off, which counts against; with 7 of 8 below my price, settle the price before reading this.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 as you said or easier · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts sign-off answers over 8 operations leads, with a 6 of 8 bar marked on the strip, and "could sign alone" counting for me is spelled out in the rule line.
screens.why_b3: "Buyer and payer" and "The contractor operations lead decides, and the CFO has to agree" are the name and line I checked going in.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the CFO in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone" tells me concretely who to put in front of the price.
screens.why_b5: The screen says "a lean, not a call" for n=8, but "the CFO in most deals" stretches 4 of 8 into most, and it doesn't flag that a belief sitting exactly at the bar would flip on one answer.
screens.instead: Just holding: 6 of 8, exactly at the bar, so one answer flips it; the CFO signs off in half the deals (4 of 8), so bring a cost case the CFO can approve, while 2 leads sign alone and 2 deals sit with someone else.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside its deciding count, 3 of 8 expecting longer than 2 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The bands, the 8 people and the for/against colouring read at once, but the bar is drawn as "6 of 8" for me on the strip while the verdict states it as "no more than 2 of 8" against, so I had to flip it to see they match.
screens.why_b3: The title is Purchase friction and the belief is my line word for word: a trial on one live job within about 2 weeks, or not needed.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of that length" points me to a month, but it doesn't say what to change, such as quoting a 30-day pilot or clearing the Procore check up front, and sends the reasons to another tab.
screens.why_b5: It calls 2 weeks to 1 month "most often" when it ties 3 to 3 with 1 to under 2 weeks, and it says a flat "Did not hold" over a one-person miss whose band starts at exactly my 2 weeks, though the count line does say it is a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Missed by one: 3 of 8 say 2 weeks to a month, against a bar of 2, and as many say 1 to 2 weeks; quote the pilot as a 30-day window and see Insights for what slows the three.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 3 short", so I know the verdict and the number behind it at once.
screens.why_b2: Three bars (3 yes, 3 probably not, 2 no) over 8 people, with the marker at 6, read at a glance; the bar is stated twice ("6 of 8" and "no more than 1 in 3 against") but the two agree.
screens.why_b3: "Commitment" and "start a paid pilot on one site now" are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say what this means for how I sell, such as dropping the paid-pilot ask for something smaller, which matters with price also failing.
screens.why_b5: n=8 is shown, all are counted, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps "did not hold" from reading as settled.
screens.instead: Only 3 of 8 ops leads would pay for a one-site pilot now, so lead with a free or discounted trial on one live job and ask for the paid site after it; see Insights for what the other 5 would start with.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up / Did not hold) with the deciding count right beside it: 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6, 3 of 8 expecting longer than 2 weeks against no more than 2, and 3 of 8 yes against 6, 3 short.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and Commitment carry the belief lines I checked word for word, and the Price line ($800 to $1,000 per site a month) is my own price band from launch.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do; I have to work out for myself that the quotes point to proving the hours saved, pricing per active super instead of per site, and a free one-job trial, and the two empty boxes give no direction at all.
screens.why_b5: The counts add up and stay visible (7 against, all 7 asked; 3 against with 2 never asked and 1 asked on Price; 5 against with 3 never asked and 2 asked on Price), and no box claims more than its few answers carry.
screens.why_b6: The quotes tell me things I did not write: buyers can't see what the logs cost them, one firm puts it at about $600 a month in overtime, per-site pricing stacks up on top of Procore, one would pay more if priced per user, one wants a free month first, and one won't trust an app with the legal record in a dispute.

screens.why1: This is the buyer's link, so showing me the idea first, before anything about price or who signs off, makes sense to me as the person who would pay for it.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, assignees, due dates, Procore and ACC are all words I use every week, and 'AI scribe' is clear enough the first time I read it.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk the job and how the notes get into Procore or ACC, so I can picture this on our sites.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The founder's idea is getting the day's photos and notes into the daily log, but the card turns it into site walk notes and texted action items and never says 'daily log', so the record-keeping point has drifted.
screens.why6: The last sentence just repeats the middle of the card, with 'Procore or ACC' said twice and 'talked-over site walk videos' a mouthful, so by the end I'd be hearing it again instead of anything new.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an AI scribe for site walks. Your superintendents take short videos and talk over them as they walk, and Fresco turns them into the daily log, with photos, sent to Procore or ACC in one click, and texts the crew their action items. The people building it believe this would save your supers the end-of-day log writing.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what the daily log costs us now in hours is the obvious place to start the buying questions.
screens.why2: Daily log is our word, but 'hours per site last month' makes me multiply a super's half hour or hour a night across about 22 workdays, and 'your team' leaves me unsure whether it means only the super or the PM and the foremen too.
screens.why3: I pay for the tools, but my supers write the logs, so I know roughly what they spend and would be guessing a monthly per-site total.
screens.why4: The number box fits, but there are two escapes, and 'None' overlaps with typing 0, which the spoken line itself says counts as none.
screens.why5: It asks plainly about time spent on the daily log, with nothing of the product or the founder's terms showing.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'a number of hours per site last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful, and 'none is 0' sounds odd when spoken.
screens.instead: Last month, about how long did a super spend on the daily log each workday, in minutes? (box: minutes a day; escape: I can't recall)

screens.why1: I've just been told what Fresco is and asked how much time the daily log eats, so asking what it's worth to me a month per site is the obvious next thing and it's exactly my call to make.
screens.why2: "Worth to you a month, per site" is how I already think about every tool we put on our jobs, so I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I sign for the software our sites run on, so I know what I'd pay per job per month for something that fills in the daily log.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and complete, but for a notes-and-photos tool my real answer sits somewhere between $50 and $300, and that all disappears into one wide "Under $500" while three of the five rungs sit above $800.
screens.why5: It still reads as the founder's monthly per-site price, and nothing about their roles or plan reaches me beyond the idea card I was meant to see.
screens.why6: The four-then-two split is easy to hold, but "Or say you can't say" trips the ear when heard once.
screens.instead: What would Fresco be worth to you a month, per site? Under $100 · $100 to under $300 · $300 to under $800 · $800 or more · I wouldn't pay for this; escape: I can't say (said aloud: "Or say: I can't say.")

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking what would push that number up is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and it repeats the band I just picked, so I know exactly what it's pointing at.
screens.why3: I'm the one who pays for our site software, so I know what would make a tool worth more to me, like covering all our jobs or pushing straight into the Procore daily log.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with no options or chips.
screens.why5: It keeps the price I gave and the name from the idea card, and nothing new about the product or who it's for slips in.
screens.why6: One short question heard once, and the band says fine aloud as five hundred to under eight hundred dollars, though adding 'a month per site' would make the echo exact.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking whether I could approve that spend myself is the obvious next thing, although the $800 is the top of my $500 to $800 band rather than what I'd actually pay.
screens.why2: Signing off on a per-site monthly spend is my everyday language, and CFO is a word every ops lead at a GC knows, even if at our size it's often the owner or controller who signs.
screens.why3: I know exactly who has to approve software spend at my company, so I can answer this straight from what I do.
screens.why4: The CFO option overlaps with 'several people would have to agree', since the CFO is usually one of those people, it lists the owner or president nowhere except under 'someone else's decision', and leading with a 'No' before the 'Yes' reads oddly.
screens.why5: The screen keeps the sign-off question and the price, and nothing of the founder's plan or role names reaches me beyond the product name I've already been shown.
screens.why6: Four short options are easy to hold when heard, but three of them start with the same 'No' and the closing 'Or say you can't say' is clumsy out loud.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month yourself, or would someone above you have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · No, the owner or CFO would have to agree · No, several people would have to agree · No, it's someone else's call; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off on $800 a site myself, asking how long the trial step would hold up the buy is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: A trial on one live job is plain to me, but 'if you bought it, how long would a trial take before it went through' reads backwards, since the trial comes before I buy and nothing 'goes through' on a trial, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I run pilots on a single job before rolling a tool out to every site, so I know about how long one takes.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover everything from under a week to over three months, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real answer if the tool sold itself, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but the 'if you bought... before it went through' frame wrapped around 'a trial on one live job' blurs whether it asks how long the pilot runs or how long the purchase waits on it.
screens.why6: One short question with four bands I can hold, then a two-way pick on my side, and the escape said last, so it says well aloud.
screens.instead: Before you bought Fresco, how long would you trial it on one live job? Under 1 week · 1 to under 2 weeks · 2 weeks to 1 month · 1 to 3 months · Over 3 months · We wouldn't trial it (escape: I can't tell)

screens.why1: After the price, who signs and how long a trial takes, asking whether I'd actually put it on a job is the obvious close.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is how I'd try any new field tool, so it reads plain first time.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides whether a new tool goes onto a job, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: The yes is firm while the no side gets two steps, so there's no 'probably yes' or 'yes, if the price is right', and that's where I'd honestly land.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea as a pilot on one site and nothing leaks beyond the card I was shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question and three short options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a paid pilot on one site, or not? Yes, I'd start one · Probably yes · Probably not · No
